title: Genuine Global Kochen-Specker Contextuality as Classical Coordination Cost
abstract: Classical simulations of quantum correlations can fail because no low-communication local hidden-variable model exists, or because no single noncontextual hidden state can explain all compatible measurement contexts. This manuscript studies a third regime: genuine global Kochen-Specker contextuality, where local subsystems are noncontextual and the tested multipartite blocks are generalized-Bell-local, but the whole empirical model admits no global noncontextual hidden-variable explanation. We propose a coordination-cost framework in which communication, memory, and local computation are treated as different ways for a classical simulator to maintain a global classical explanation from locally available information. We introduce coordination bits, global contextual covering numbers, scaling laws for task families, and an abstract lifting theorem showing how classical simulation lower bounds for KS-contextual seed families can be transferred to genuinely global-KS models. As worked examples, we analyze a polarization-path Hardy obstruction and postselected KCBS-type tasks.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive framework to measure genuine global contextuality using 'coordination costs,' quantifying the minimum required classical communication and memory. By relating this cost to combinatorial covering numbers ($\chi_G$), it establishes that strong quantum contextuality imposes unavoidable lower bounds on any classical simulation protocol. This advances the understanding of resource separation between quantum and classical physics.
main_problem: To establish a quantitative link between genuine global Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality and the minimum classical coordination cost required to simulate quantum correlations.
main_result: The paper proves that genuine global KS contextuality lower-bounds a joint classical coordination cost involving communication, memory, and local computation depth ($B+M \ge \log_2 \chi_G(T)$).
method: It develops an abstract framework using compiled task models and resource inequalities derived from covering numbers ($\chi_D^G$) to quantify the required classical resources.
model_or_system: The analysis uses abstract information-theoretic models, generalizing Bell nonlocality (communication cost) and KS contextuality into a joint coordination cost for arbitrary constraint satisfaction tasks.
key_observables: Global contextual covering number ($\chi_G(T)$), depth-restricted covering number ($\chi_D^G(T)$), and the classical resource tuple $(B, M, D)$.
important_parameters: Coordination bits (the common unit of cost), repetition factor ($m$), and flag probabilities ($p_{F,n}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on defining a 'cover-admissible' classical simulator model and assumes the existence of an abstract lifting theorem to transfer bounds from simple KS seeds to global models.
figures_summary: Not specified (Notes describe mathematical theorems and derived inequalities rather than figure content).
paper_structure: The paper builds logically by first defining the resource cost framework, then introducing specific combinatorial tasks (like twisted hypercubes or Hardy games) to derive concrete lower bounds on $\chi_G(T)$, culminating in an abstract theorem that transfers these bounds from simple contextuality seeds to genuinely global models.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical tool—the coordination cost—to quantify the computational resources needed by classical simulators to mimic quantum correlations, which is fundamental for understanding resource limitations in quantum computation and communication protocols.
